title: Repair a damaged extension cord or power lead
summary: Cut out the damaged part of a mains extension cord and fit a new plug or socket, or make two shorter cords. Get the wire colours right, clamp the outer sheath, and test with a meter before plugging in.

materials.item: Rewireable plug and/or socket, rated at least as high as the cord
Donor cord of the same or thicker wire

steps.text: Unplug both ends. Inspect the whole cord: cuts, crushed or flattened spots, bare copper, melted or scorched plugs.
steps.warn: Never handle or repair a cord that is plugged in.

steps.text: Decide the fix. Damage near an end: cut it off and fit a new plug or socket. Damage in the middle: cut it there and fit a new plug and socket to make two shorter cords. A spliced middle is a last resort.
Cut the cord well past any damage, at least 5 cm into undamaged cord.

Open the new plug or socket and see how much outer sheath it needs inside. Strip that much sheath (usually 3–5 cm) by scoring around it lightly with a knife and bending, without cutting the inner insulation.
Strip about 1 cm from each inner wire. Twist the strands tight.

Identify the wires. North America: black is hot, white is neutral, green is ground. Europe and UK: brown is live, blue is neutral, green-and-yellow is earth. Older cords may differ; trace each wire to the other end with a meter if unsure.

Connect them. Hot or live goes to the brass or narrow-blade terminal (or L). Neutral goes to the silver or wide-blade terminal (or N). Ground or earth goes to the green screw (or E or the earth symbol). Wrap wires clockwise round screws, or push fully into clamps. No stray strands.
Leave the ground or earth wire a little longer than the others so it is the last to pull free if the cord is yanked.
Clamp the outer sheath in the cord grip so the grip takes any pull, not the wire terminals. Close up the plug.
Test with the meter on continuity or ohms: each pin to its matching socket hole at the other end should beep; no pair of different pins should beep.
steps.warn: If any two different conductors connect, or the ground doesn't, don't use the cord.

steps.text: If you must splice: stagger the joins so they don't sit side by side, crimp or solder each, cover each with heat-shrink, then cover the whole splice. Keep spliced cords out of wet places and from under rugs.
steps.warn: A taped splice can overheat or short. Check it for warmth when first used under load.

notes:
## How much a cord can carry

| Wire size | Typical rating |
|---|---|
| 18 AWG (about 0.75 mm²) | about 7–10 A: lamps and small loads only |
| 16 AWG (about 1.0–1.5 mm²) | about 10–13 A |
| 14 AWG (about 2.0–2.5 mm²) | about 15 A |
| 12 AWG (about 3.3–4 mm²) | about 20 A |

The rating is usually printed on the sheath. A cord's plug and socket must be rated at least as high as the cord. UK-style plugs hold a fuse: fit 13 A for heavy cords and 3 A for thin lamp flex.

## Good habits

- Uncoil a cord fully before running a heavy load (a heater, a kettle, a welder). A coiled cord can overheat and melt.
- Long thin cords drop voltage. Motors on long thin cords run hot and weak. Use the shortest, thickest cord you have.
- Check plugs for warmth after an hour of heavy use. Warm means a loose connection or an overloaded cord.
- Throw away cords with melted plugs or brittle, cracked sheathing. Strip them for wire.

## Generators

When running from a generator, use a cord thick enough for the full load, and keep the generator outdoors and away from doors and windows (see safety_carbon_monoxide).
